section.title: Repentance and the Lament over Jerusalem
section.sectionRationale: Told of Galileans slaughtered by Pilate, Jesus refuses to rank victims by guilt and instead presses the same summons on everyone: unless you repent, you too will perish. A barren fig tree is spared one more year of patient tending, a bent woman is freed on the Sabbath, and the kingdom is likened to a mustard seed and to leaven, small beginnings that fill the earth. The chapter closes as Jesus, resolute toward Jerusalem, weeps over the city that kills its prophets and refuses to be gathered.
section.thesis: The kingdom presses its call to repentance on every hearer, offers one more season of patient grace, frees the bound even on the Sabbath, grows unstoppably from small beginnings, and comes at last as the tears of a Savior over a city that would not be gathered.
section.frameNote: Six movements: the call to repentance; the barren fig tree; the bent woman set free; the mustard seed and the leaven; the narrow door; and the lament over Jerusalem.

units.label: A call to repentance
units.note: unless you repent, you too will perish

verses.text: At that time some of those present told Jesus about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices.
To this He replied, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered this way?
No, I tell you. But unless you {{metanoeo|repent}}, you too will all perish.
Or those eighteen who were killed when the tower of Siloam collapsed on them: Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem?
No, I tell you. But unless you {{metanoeo|repent}}, you too will all perish.”

units.label: The barren fig tree
units.note: leave it alone again this year

verses.text: Then Jesus told this parable: “A man had a fig tree that was planted in his vineyard. He went to look for fruit on it but did not find any.

So he said to the keeper of the vineyard, ‘Look, for the past three years I have come to search for fruit on this fig tree and haven’t found any. Therefore cut it down! Why should it use up the soil?’
‘Sir,’ the man replied, ‘leave it alone again this year, until I dig around it and fertilize it.
If it bears fruit next year, fine. But if not, you can cut it down.’”

units.label: The bent woman set free
units.note: should she not be released on the Sabbath

verses.text: One Sabbath Jesus was teaching in one of the synagogues,
and a woman there had been disabled by a spirit for eighteen years. She was hunched over and could not stand up straight.
When Jesus saw her, He called her over and said, “Woman, you are set free from your disability.”
Then He placed His hands on her, and immediately she straightened up and began to glorify God.
But the synagogue leader was indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath. “There are six days for work,” he told the crowd. “So come and be healed on those days and not on the Sabbath.”
“You hypocrites!” the Lord replied. “Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or donkey from the stall and lead it to water?
Then should not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has kept bound for eighteen long years, be released from her bondage on the Sabbath day?”
When Jesus said this, all His adversaries were humiliated. And the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things He was doing.

units.label: The mustard seed and the leaven
units.note: small beginnings that fill the earth

verses.text: Then Jesus asked, “What is the {{basileia|kingdom}} of God like? To what can I compare it?
It is like a mustard seed that a man tossed into his garden. It grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air nested in its branches.”
Again He asked, “To what can I compare the kingdom of God?
It is like leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour, until all of it was leavened.”
Then Jesus traveled throughout the towns and villages, teaching as He made His way toward Jerusalem.
“Lord,” someone asked Him, “will only a few people be saved?” Jesus answered,
“Make every effort to enter through the {{stenos|narrow door}}. For many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able.
After the master of the house gets up and shuts the door, you will stand outside knocking and saying, ‘Lord, open the door for us.’ But he will reply, ‘I do not know where you are from.’
Then you will say, ‘We ate and drank with you, and you taught in our streets.’
And he will answer, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you are from. Depart from me, all you evildoers.’
There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth when you see Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but you yourselves are thrown out.
People will come from east and west and north and south, and will recline at the table in the kingdom of God.
And indeed, some who are last will be first, and some who are first will be last.”

units.label: The lament over Jerusalem
units.note: how often I have longed to gather your children

verses.text: At that very hour, some Pharisees came to Jesus and told Him, “Leave this place and get away, because Herod wants to kill You.”
But Jesus replied, “Go tell that fox, ‘Look, I will keep driving out demons and healing people today and tomorrow, and on the third day I will {{teleioo|reach My goal}}.’
Nevertheless, I must keep going today and tomorrow and the next day, for it is not admissible for a prophet to perish outside of Jerusalem.

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to {{episynago|gather}} your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!
Look, your house is left to you desolate. And I tell you that you will not see Me again until you say, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

metanoeo.gloss: To repent, literally to change one's mind, to turn the whole self around. Jesus refuses to treat disaster as a scoreboard of guilt and turns the question back on His hearers: the urgent issue is not why they died but whether you will turn. Repentance is not mere regret but a reorientation of life toward God.

basileia.gloss: Kingdom, kingship, reign. The kingdom of God begins as small as a mustard seed and as hidden as leaven in dough, yet it grows into a tree and works through the whole batch. Its beginnings look unimpressive, but its end fills the earth.

stenos.gloss: Narrow, confined. The door into the kingdom is narrow, and Jesus urges His hearers to strive to enter while it stands open. The narrowness is not stinginess but urgency: there is one way in, and the time to enter is now, before the master shuts the door.

teleioo.gloss: To complete, to finish, to bring to the goal. On the third day, Jesus says, He will be perfected, a word Luke uses for the completion of His mission in death and resurrection. The threats of Herod cannot hurry or halt a course fixed by God toward Jerusalem.

episynago.gloss: To gather together, as a hen gathers her chicks. The word carries the tenderness of God longing to shelter His people under His wings, and the grief of a love refused: how often I have longed to gather you, but you were unwilling.

basic.context: People bring Jesus news of a massacre, expecting Him to explain who deserved it. He refuses to rank the dead and instead warns everyone: unless you repent, you too will perish. He tells of a barren fig tree given one more year of patient care before it is cut down. On a Sabbath He frees a woman bent double for eighteen years, and when the synagogue leader objects, He exposes the hypocrisy of caring more for an ox than for a suffering daughter of Abraham. He pictures the kingdom as a mustard seed and as leaven, tiny beginnings that grow to fill everything. He warns that the door is narrow and will one day shut. And He weeps over Jerusalem, longing to gather her like a hen gathers her chicks, but she was unwilling.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the chapter as one sustained call to repent while there is still time. The disasters, the barren tree, and the narrow door all press the same urgency; the healing and the parables show the kingdom's grace and growth; the lament reveals the heart of God behind the warnings, grieving over a people who will not come.
basic.originalLanguages: The key verb is metanoeo, to repent, to turn the whole life around. The basileia, the kingdom, grows from the smallest seed. The door is stenos, narrow, and open only for now. Jesus says He will teleioo, be perfected, on the third day, His mission completed in death and resurrection. And He longs to episynago, to gather, His people as a hen gathers her chicks.
basic.typology: The barren fig tree recalls Israel as God's unfruitful vineyard, and looks ahead to the withered fig tree of Holy Week. The bent woman freed on the Sabbath pictures the true Sabbath rest Jesus brings. The hen gathering her chicks echoes the God who shelters His people under His wings in the Psalms.
basic.christ: Jesus is the patient keeper of the vineyard who pleads for one more year of grace, the Lord of the Sabbath who unbinds what Satan has bound, and the resolute Savior who cannot be scared off His road to Jerusalem by Herod the fox. Above all He is the God of Israel come in person, weeping over the city and longing to gather her children.
basic.god: God is patient, giving the barren tree another season; He is compassionate, freeing the bound even on His holy day; He is sovereign, growing His kingdom from nothing; and He is heartbroken love, longing to gather a people who refuse Him. His warnings and His tears come from the same heart.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 5 sings of Israel as a vineyard that yields no fruit. Psalm 91 speaks of finding refuge under God's wings. Matthew 7 sets the narrow gate against the wide road. Romans 2 warns that God's patience is meant to lead us to repentance.
basic.oneStory: As Jesus sets His face toward Jerusalem, He presses the whole nation, and every reader, to turn while the door stands open. The kingdom is quietly filling the earth, and the King Himself weeps over the city that will not be gathered, on His way to the cross that will open the door wide.

context.literary:
Luke 13 begins and ends in Jerusalem, though Jesus is still far away in verse 1. The chapter's opening is a pair of news items, Pilate's massacre and the falling tower, and its close is the lament over the city, so the whole is bracketed by the fate of Jerusalem and by a warning about perishing. Between those brackets lie two parables of fruit and growth, the fig tree and the pair of mustard seed and leaven, and two scenes of confrontation, the synagogue healing and the exchange about the narrow door. The movement runs from a call to repentance, through a delay of judgment, to a sharper warning that the door will shut, and finally to the grief of the one who stands outside the city and longs for it.

The parables seem to look in two directions. The fig tree is a parable of delay and fruit, directed at the individual and the nation, and it carries a threat. The mustard seed and the leaven, told straight after the healing of the bent woman, are parables of hidden growth and carry a promise. The first is a question about whether there will be fruit, and the second is about whether the kingdom will come, and Luke places them next to each other so that the reader hears both. Judgment is not the whole message, and the kingdom's growth is not a reason to presume.

There are also echoes inside the chapter. The 'eighteen' who died at Siloam in verse 4 are matched by the 'eighteen years' of the woman's bondage in verses 11 and 16, though the coincidence is not built upon. The Sabbath leader's complaint about the six days of work, verse 14, is answered by the 'ox or donkey' of verse 15 and by the thought that this woman has waited long enough. Three times in the chapter someone speaks about who will be 'in' and who 'out': the crowd at the door, the Gentiles who come from the four directions, and the city whose house is left desolate. The chapter finally asks who will be gathered, and who is unwilling.
context.historical:
The report in verse 1 concerns an act of violence by Pilate, who governed Judea as prefect from about AD 26 to 36. Josephus tells of other violent episodes under Pilate but this particular killing, in which Galilean worshippers were slain as they offered their sacrifices, is not recorded outside Luke. Galileans were often under suspicion of unrest, and the people who told Jesus perhaps expected Him to say that such victims were punished for something. The second event, the tower at Siloam, a pool in the south of Jerusalem, John 9:7, was an accident, not a crime. Together the two cover violence done by people and disaster that no one planned, and Jesus rejects the idea that either exposes the victims as worse sinners than others.

The fig tree stands in a vineyard, a common arrangement in Israel's farms, and a man who had waited three years for fruit had good reason for his patience to run out. The vinedresser's request for a year is a request for a final season of digging and manuring. Israel's prophets used the fig tree and the vine as pictures of the nation, and a tree that bore no fruit was a symbol of judgment, Hosea 9:10, Jeremiah 8:13, Micah 7:1.

The synagogue scene reflects the sabbath debate recorded throughout the Gospels. The leader's complaint draws on the commandment to labour for six days and rest on the seventh, Exodus 20:9-10, and he treats healing as work. Jesus' reply draws on a custom everyone acknowledged, that animals were untied and led to water on the Sabbath. The woman is called a 'daughter of Abraham,' a title that asserts her place in the covenant people and that parallels Zacchaeus as a 'son of Abraham' in Luke 19:9. Her stoop, which the text attributes to a spirit, was permanent and visible, and the whole synagogue knew her.

The warning from the Pharisees in verse 31 shows that Jesus was in the territory of Herod Antipas, who ruled Galilee and Perea and who had put John the Baptist in prison and then killed him, Luke 3:19-20 and 9:9. Calling Antipas a fox is probably a comment on his cunning and smallness. Jesus' insistence on going on to Jerusalem is the reason He will not turn aside, and His statement that a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem is full of irony: the holy city has a long record of killing prophets, as the case of Uriah in Jeremiah 26:20-23 shows.
context.canonical:
The fig tree belongs to a long line of prophetic images of Israel as an unproductive plant. Isaiah 5:1-7 sings of a vineyard planted on a fertile hill that yielded wild grapes, and its conclusion is that the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel and that He looked for justice but saw bloodshed. Hosea 9:10 found Israel like grapes in the wilderness and like the firstfruits of the fig tree, only to find them following Baal-peor. Jesus takes up the same picture, and in the Holy Week scene of Mark 11:12-14 and 20-21, and Matthew 21:19, He acts it out on a tree that bears only leaves and then withers.

The mustard seed grows into a tree where birds nest, and that picture echoes Ezekiel 17:22-24, 31:6 and Daniel 4:10-12, where great trees shelter the birds and the nations. Whatever else the nesting birds suggest, they appear in a prophetic image for a kingdom that shelters the peoples. The leaven is usually a negative picture in Scripture, Exodus 12:15 and Luke 12:1, so its positive use here is deliberately unexpected. The three measures of flour recall Genesis 18:6, when Abraham told Sarah to bake bread from three seahs for his heavenly visitors.

The door scene draws on Psalm 6:8, 'Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity,' and on the great feast of Isaiah 25:6-8, which gathers all peoples. The four directions of verse 29 echo Psalm 107:3 and Isaiah 43:5. The lament over Jerusalem uses the Old Testament's wing imagery for God's protection, Deuteronomy 32:11, Ruth 2:12 and Psalms 17:8 and 36:7. Its closing citation of Psalm 118:26, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD,' is sung at the Triumphal Entry in Luke 19:38, and the desolate house recalls Jeremiah 22:5. Matthew places a nearly identical lament in Matthew 23:37-39.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers to take two truths at once and refuse to dilute either. The first is that repentance is urgent for everyone. Jesus will not let the questioners treat the Galileans' deaths as a puzzle about other people's guilt, and the lesson He draws, twice, is about the hearers: 'unless you repent, you too will all perish.' The second truth is that God is astonishingly patient and tender. The vinedresser pleads for one more year, the woman is freed on a Sabbath, the kingdom grows like a seed under the soil, and the lament shows the heart of the one who warns.

The chapter is aimed at hearers who believe they are safe because of their heritage or association. 'We ate and drank with you, and you taught in our streets' is the plea of people who had been near Jesus and were not His. Luke's first readers, many of them Gentiles, would have heard the promise that people will come from the four directions to sit at the table, and the warning that some who expect to be at the table will not be. He writes to make his readers look to their own fruit, and to give them courage that the kingdom is moving in spite of its small beginnings.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Several things here are narration, not command. The slaughter of the Galileans and the fall of the tower are events Jesus responds to, and He does not teach that suffering is never connected to sin, only that the connection cannot be read off the victims. John 9:2-3 shows the same restraint. The Sabbath healing is an event, and the principle drawn from it, that releasing a person from bondage is fitting on the Sabbath, is prescriptive for how the day's meaning is read, since the Sabbath's own rationale in Deuteronomy 5:15 is deliverance from slavery.

The parables of the fig tree, the seed and the leaven describe how God deals with the world and are not instructions about gardening or baking. The command in verse 24, 'Make every effort to enter through the narrow door,' is plainly prescriptive, and so is the call to repent. The warning that the door will be shut is a statement of fact about the end of opportunity, and Jesus uses it to compel action now. The lament in verses 34 and 35 is a window into the heart of Jesus, and its application is to take His grief seriously and to receive the gathering He offers, and it does not provide a formula for predicting the future of any nation or city.

debates.question: What does Jesus mean by 'unless you repent, you too will all perish'?

views.label: A call to turn to God to escape final judgment
views.case: Jesus severs the link between particular tragedies and particular guilt, then universalizes the danger; the perishing in view is ultimate ruin under God's judgment, escaped only by genuine repentance. The barren fig tree that faces the axe confirms the stakes.

views.label: A warning of national catastrophe on Jerusalem
views.case: Some read the perishing as the coming destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, when many Jews indeed perished; the lament over the city and its desolate house point that way. Yet this reading, while historically real, need not exclude the deeper and universal call to repentance.

debates.bearing: Whether one hears an ultimate or a historical warning, the summons is the same and it falls on us: turn to God now, for no one is exempt and the door will not stand open forever.

debates.question: Does the narrow door mean only a few will be saved?

views.label: The question is redirected from counting to entering
views.case: Asked whether few are saved, Jesus does not give a number but a command: make every effort to enter. He then pictures people streaming from every direction to the feast, so the emphasis falls not on scarcity but on the urgency of entering the one door while it is open.

views.label: The saved are genuinely few and the way is hard
views.case: The narrowness of the door and the warning that many will try and fail suggest that entry is costly and that presumption, We ate and drank with you, saves no one. The way is real and demanding, not a broad and easy path.

debates.bearing: Both guard against complacency: salvation is neither a matter of casual belonging nor of idle speculation, but of striving to enter through the one narrow door that is Christ Himself, while grace still holds it open.

debates.question: What does 'you will not see Me again until you say, Blessed is He who comes' promise?

views.label: The welcome at the Triumphal Entry
views.case: Luke 19:38 records the crowds crying 'Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!' as Jesus enters the city. Some hold that this fulfils the saying, with the further point that the same city that welcomed Him with palms turned on Him within days.

views.label: A future welcome at His return
views.case: The saying says the city will not see Him again until it speaks the blessing, and the crowd that sang in Luke 19 did not see the Jesus who was then arrested. Many read it as pointing to the final return, when the people will receive the one they rejected, and some connect it to Paul's expectation in Romans 11:25-26 that Israel will be saved.

views.label: A judgment-and-hope saying with both in view
views.case: The verse is a verdict on the house, which is left desolate, and also a door left ajar by the word 'until.' Luke 19:41-44 and 21:20 show the first half coming true in the siege of the city, and the 'until' keeps the hope alive.

debates.bearing: All three readings agree on the structure: judgment now, with a promise that the blessing Psalm 118:26 describes will one day be said. The practical force for the reader is the same as the whole chapter's, which is to say the blessing now, while the door stands open.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb that drives the first half of the chapter is metanoeo, 'repent,' verses 3 and 5. It joins meta, which suggests change, and noeo, to think or perceive, and it means a re-orientation of the whole mind that issues in changed living. In Luke the word is linked with fruit, as in Luke 3:8, 'Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance,' and the fig tree parable that follows is its picture. The verb for 'perish,' apollymi, is the verb that appears in the three parables of loss in Luke 15 for the sheep, the coin and the son who were lost. So the 'perishing' threatened here is the very loss that the shepherd, the woman and the father go out to prevent.

In the fig tree parable the vinedresser says 'leave it alone,' verse 8, using aphes, the imperative of aphiemi, the verb that Luke uses everywhere for forgiving and releasing. The request for a stay of execution is, in the wording, a plea to forgive and let go for another season. The same family of words appears in the Sabbath scene. Jesus says to the woman, 'you are set free,' apolelysai, a perfect passive of apolyo, meaning that she has been released and remains released. In verse 16 He says she was 'bound,' edesen, and that she should have been 'loosed,' lythenai, introduced by ouk edei, 'was it not necessary?' So the Sabbath, Jesus says, is exactly the right day for loosing, a theme that echoes His programme in Luke 4:18, which mentions the release of the oppressed.

The leaven, in verse 21, is 'mixed in,' but the Greek verb is enekrypsen, 'hid,' which is the same word Matthew uses. The kingdom is the kind of thing that is hidden in the dough and works unseen. The narrow door comes with the verb agonizomai, 'make every effort,' in verse 24, from which we get 'agony.' The word belongs to athletic contests and battles, and it pictures effort and struggle, though the effort is the response of those who enter through a door that someone else provides. The answer of the householder in verse 25, 'I do not know where you are from,' says that familiarity is not the same as relationship, a line echoed in Matthew 7:23.

In verse 32 Jesus says that on the third day teleioumai, 'I reach My goal.' The verb teleioo means to complete or bring to an end, and the present passive form can be read as 'I am being brought to completion.' The same verb is used in Hebrews 2:10, where the author of salvation is made perfect through suffering. Finally the lament has a wordplay in verse 34: 'I longed,' ethelesa, 'but you were unwilling,' ouk ethelesate. The same verb, 'to will,' belongs to both parties, and the sentence sets the will of the Lord against the refusal of the city.

typology.type: The unfruitful vine and the barren fig tree, Isaiah 5:1-7 and Luke 13:6-9
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah's song of the vineyard, in which the LORD looked for justice and found bloodshed, shapes the whole parable. The owner has come looking for fruit for three years. Jesus tells it in the shadow of Jerusalem and the temple, and the withering of the tree in Mark 11:20-21 shows what happens to fruitless religion. In Christ the true vine appears, John 15:1, and those who abide in Him bear fruit, John 15:5. The type falls short because the vinedresser's patience in Luke 13 is a delay, not a cancellation. The final verdict is left open, and the story stops before the next year ends.

typology.type: The woman loosed on the Sabbath, Deuteronomy 5:12-15
typology.fulfillment: The second giving of the Sabbath commandment grounds it in deliverance: 'Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt,' Deuteronomy 5:15. A woman bound for eighteen years is released on the Sabbath and called a daughter of Abraham, and the day of rest is shown to be the right day for freedom. Christ is the one who says, 'if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed,' John 8:36, and who offers the rest that the weekly Sabbath pointed to, Matthew 11:28. The type falls short in that it concerns one woman and one body, whereas Christ's liberation reaches to the bondage of sin and death, Romans 6:18.

typology.type: The great tree in which birds nest, Ezekiel 17:22-24
typology.fulfillment: The LORD promises to take a shoot and plant it on the high mountain of Israel, and it will become a majestic cedar under which birds of every kind will nest. Jesus' mustard seed starts almost invisible and grows large enough for the birds to shelter in it, and Daniel 4:12 has the same scene of a tree sheltering the creatures of the earth. Christ is the seed that falls into the ground and dies and then bears much fruit, John 12:24, and the church grows from Him until it includes people from every nation. The type falls short if it is read as an earthly empire, since the kingdom of God grows by the word and the Spirit.

typology.type: The hen and her chicks, Psalm 36:7 and Deuteronomy 32:11
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament speaks of God's protection as a bird's wings, 'the shadow of Your wings,' Psalm 36:7, and as an eagle hovering over its young, Deuteronomy 32:11. Ruth took refuge under the LORD's wings, Ruth 2:12. Jesus takes the role of the one who longs to gather, so that the saying becomes a claim to be the God of Israel in person. In Christ the hen's protection is shown at its limit: He gathers by going to the place where the chicks' enemies strike, the cross. The type falls short as an image of power, since the hen can only shelter those who come, and Jesus speaks of a gathering that the city refuses.

study.christ:
The chapter shows Christ in His patience, His authority over bondage, His determination and His grief, and each of these is tied to verses in the text. In the fig tree parable the one who pleads for another year can be heard as a picture of His intercession, though the parable does not identify the characters. What it does show is a gardener who is willing to dig and manure, to spend labour on a tree that has given nothing, and it fits with the intercession of Christ that Hebrews 7:25 describes.

In the Sabbath scene He is the one who says, 'Woman, you are set free,' and lays His hands on her, and she straightens at once. This is a sign of His programme in Luke 4:18, and it is also a claim about the Sabbath: when Jesus calls her a daughter of Abraham whom Satan has bound, He is declaring that a day made for rest and deliverance is the best day for His work. He brings the day's purpose to its goal, and He does so with the authority of one who is Lord of it.

In verses 31 to 33 He is utterly resolute. The Pharisees warn Him that Herod wants to kill Him, and He answers with a timetable no tyrant controls, 'today and tomorrow, and on the third day I will reach My goal.' The words speak first of a short run of ministry. For the reader of Luke, who knows what is coming, the third day carries a deeper sound, and the same Gospel later reports the angels saying that He must rise on the third day, Luke 24:7. Jesus walks to Jerusalem because 'it is not admissible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem,' an ironic remark that presents the cross as the place where the sequence of killed prophets comes to its end.

In the lament He speaks as the God of Israel. The one who 'longed to gather your children' is the one who in the Psalms spreads His wings over His people. He does not speak as a prophet only reporting God's grief but in the first person, as the one who sent the prophets and who has wanted to gather the city again and again. The desolate house is left to the city, and yet He ends with the promise that they will see Him again when they say the blessing. That makes Jesus both the judge who closes the door and the Saviour who holds it open, and Luke is careful to leave both in view.
study.god:
God appears in this chapter as patient, as compassionate and as grieved, and the chapter holds these together with His holiness. His patience is shown in the vinedresser's year. He is not slow to act, as 2 Peter 3:9 puts it, but is patient with people because He does not want anyone to perish, and Romans 2:4 says His kindness is meant to lead us to repentance. The patience of God is not the same as indifference. The tree has a last year, and the door will eventually shut.

His compassion shows in His readiness to meet suffering on the day that the leaders considered sacred. The woman did not ask for healing. Jesus saw her and called her over. The God of this chapter takes the initiative toward the afflicted, and His mercy is not delayed by religious scruple. In the Sabbath's own rationale in Deuteronomy 5:15, God is the one who brings slaves out, and the day of rest is a memorial to His freeing work.

His sovereignty is shown in the growth of the kingdom from an unnoticed beginning. The seed is thrown into the garden, the leaven is hidden in the flour, and the result is not a matter of human strategy. The same sovereignty draws people from the four corners of the earth to the table in verse 29, and reverses ranks, so that the last are first and the first last. It is not an arbitrary reversal, since the criterion is entry through the narrow door, which is a matter of response and not heritage.

God's holiness stands behind the shut door. The householder who says 'I do not know where you are from' and who orders evildoers away is speaking in the language of Psalm 6:8. Holiness does not cancel love, however. The lament of verse 34 reveals a God who longs, and who respects the will He has made. That is the hardest thing in the chapter: 'you were unwilling.' God does not force the gathering. For worship, the chapter calls us to bow before the God who is both patient and just, to receive His warnings as the tears of a Father, and to come under His wings while there is time.

crossReferences.note: The vineyard song ends with the LORD looking for justice and finding bloodshed. Jesus' parable of the fig tree draws on the same picture of a planted, tended, and unfruitful Israel. The song ends in judgment, and Jesus' version leaves one more year, which shows God's patience in a text that otherwise carries only warning.

God found Israel like the firstfruits of the fig tree in its first season, and then they went after Baal-peor. The prophet recalls the delight of early days and the failure that followed. The fig tree in the Luke parable is a later chapter of the same story, and the owner's search for fruit is the LORD's own.

This version of the Sabbath commandment rests on the exodus: remember that you were a slave and the LORD brought you out. The bent woman's release on the Sabbath does exactly what the day was given to commemorate. Jesus answers the synagogue leader out of the commandment itself.

Jesus' first sermon in Nazareth announced liberty for the captives and release for the oppressed. The healing in Luke 13 is that sermon in action, and the release language of that sermon matches the loosing of verse 16 here. It shows that this was not an exceptional miracle but His mission.

The LORD plants a shoot on Israel's mountain heights, and it becomes a majestic cedar where birds of every kind nest. The mustard seed's tree repeats the image with a smaller, humbler beginning, and the nesting birds suggest that the kingdom becomes a shelter for the nations.

Abraham asked Sarah to bake bread from three seahs of fine flour for his heavenly visitors. The woman's three measures of flour in verse 21 are the same large quantity. The size of the batch suggests a feast, and fits the picture of leaven working through all of it until it is fully leavened.

David cries out, 'Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity,' because the LORD has heard his weeping. Jesus puts the same words on the lips of the householder in verse 27. The echo implies that those shut out are the very people the psalm describes, who claimed closeness but practised wrongdoing.

The redeemed of the LORD are 'gathered from the lands, from east and west, from north and south.' The four directions of Luke 13:29 repeat that line, and apply it to people who sit at the table of the kingdom beside Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so the prophecy of regathering is read as including the nations.

Uriah the prophet spoke against the city as Jeremiah did, and King Jehoiakim had him brought back from Egypt and killed. This is one of the examples behind Jesus' claim that Jerusalem kills the prophets. The earlier slaughter helps explain why He says it is not admissible for a prophet to perish elsewhere.

The children of men take refuge in the shadow of God's wings. The hen's wings in verse 34 give the psalm's image a face in Jesus, who offers just that shelter to a city. Refuge is available, but only to those who come in under it.

Paul asks whether we disregard the riches of God's kindness, tolerance and patience, not realizing that His kindness leads us to repentance. It is a direct comment on the fig tree's extra year and gives a theology for it: the delay is a gift meant to bring about repentance, and it is not leniency.

As Jesus approaches Jerusalem He weeps over it and tells it that its enemies will hem it in. The lament of Luke 13:34-35 is looking ahead to this scene, in which the longing turns into tears and the warning into a prediction. Reading them side by side shows the grief of the judge.

study.oneStory:
This chapter belongs to the part of the story in which the LORD comes to the people He planted and looks for fruit. From the garden God had put humanity in a place to tend and to keep, Genesis 2:15, and from Abraham He had made a people to bless the families of the earth, Genesis 12:3. Israel was a vine brought out of Egypt, Psalm 80:8, and the prophets' long complaint is that the vine bore wild grapes. Luke 13 is the moment when the owner arrives with a last offer. The tree gets another year, and the question is whether it will bear.

The chapter also gathers the strands of exile and return. The prophets promised that people would come from east and west to be gathered by the LORD, and the table of Luke 13:29 is that promise made concrete, with the surprise that the people gathered include many who were never counted. The kingdom starts small, a seed and a pinch of leaven, as Israel itself began with one man and one barren wife, and its growth into a tree for the birds recalls the promise that the nations would find shelter in it. The reversal that the last will be first is built on the whole shape of the biblical story, where the younger is chosen over the older, the barren woman over the fertile, and the stranger over the insider.

It looks forward too. Jerusalem, the city of the great King, becomes the place where prophets die, and Jesus goes there anyway. The lament stands at the point where the story must pass through judgment on the city and through the cross. Its closing promise, that they will see Him again when they say 'Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord,' points to the end, when every tongue confesses Him, Philippians 2:10-11. In Revelation 21:4 God wipes away every tear, and the hen's longing is finally satisfied when the gathered people dwell under the shelter of His presence. The door that stands open now is the door that opens onto that world.

quiz.q: How does Jesus respond to the news of the Galileans killed by Pilate?

options.text: He denies that the victims were worse sinners and calls everyone to repent or likewise perish.
options.note: Luke 13:2-5 refuses to rank guilt and turns the warning on all His hearers.

options.text: He warns that Jerusalem itself faces coming judgment.
options.note: True to the chapter's later lament, but here the direct point is the universal call to repent.

options.text: He explains the hidden sins that caused the tragedy.
options.note: Jesus does the opposite; He refuses to treat the disaster as a scoreboard of particular guilt.

options.text: He assures them the victims deserved exactly what they got.
options.note: He explicitly denies that they were worse sinners than anyone else.

quiz.q: What does the parable of the barren fig tree teach?

options.text: God grants a season of patient grace and tending, but fruitless life still faces judgment.
options.note: Luke 13:6-9 holds patience and warning together: one more year, then the axe.

options.text: God is patient and gives more time to bear fruit.
options.note: True, but it leaves out the warning that unfruitfulness finally meets judgment.

options.text: God will always spare the tree no matter what.
options.note: The reprieve is for one more year, not an unconditional guarantee.

options.text: Fruitfulness does not matter to God.
options.note: The whole point is that the owner comes looking for fruit and finds none.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus heal the bent woman on the Sabbath despite the objection?

options.text: Because a daughter of Abraham bound by Satan should surely be released on the Sabbath, the day of rest and freedom.
options.note: Luke 13:15-16 grounds the healing in the Sabbath's own meaning of release.

options.text: Because He is Lord of the Sabbath and exposes their hypocrisy.
options.note: True and implied, but the stated reason centers on the woman's release as a daughter of Abraham.

options.text: Because the Sabbath law did not really apply to healing.
options.note: Jesus does not dismiss the Sabbath; He reveals its true purpose of mercy and release.

options.text: Because the synagogue leader had given Him permission.
options.note: The leader was indignant and opposed the healing.

quiz.q: What do the mustard seed and the leaven reveal about the kingdom of God?

options.text: It begins small and hidden yet grows to fill and transform everything.
options.note: Luke 13:18-21 pairs tiny beginnings with pervasive, unstoppable growth.

options.text: It grows slowly over a long period of time.
options.note: Growth is real, but the point is the contrast between small beginnings and vast end.

options.text: It stays small and unnoticed in the world.
options.note: The opposite: the seed becomes a tree and the leaven fills the whole batch.

options.text: It arrives suddenly, full-grown, with no small beginning.
options.note: Both parables stress the smallness of the beginning.

quiz.q: What does Jesus' lament over Jerusalem reveal?

options.text: The grieving love of God who longed to gather His people, met by their unwillingness.
options.note: Luke 13:34 shows tender divine longing refused by the city.

options.text: That Jerusalem would be judged and left desolate.
options.note: True to verse 35, but the heart of the lament is God's grieving love, not only the judgment.

options.text: That Jesus was afraid of Herod's threats.
options.note: He calls Herod a fox and presses on resolutely; fear is not the point.

options.text: That God had given up on His people entirely.
options.note: The longing to gather and the hope of a future 'Blessed is He who comes' show enduring love.

questions: Jesus refuses to rank the Galileans as worse sinners and instead says, unless you repent. Where do you find yourself explaining other people's suffering rather than hearing God's call to turn?
The barren tree was given one more year of patient tending. Where has God been patient with you, and what fruit is He waiting to see?
Jesus freed a woman bent double for eighteen years and called her a daughter of Abraham. Is there a long-standing bondage you have stopped believing Christ could loosen?
The door is narrow and open now, but it will one day shut. What would it mean to make every effort to enter today rather than presuming on a later time?
Jesus wept over a city that would not be gathered. Where might you be resisting the sheltering love of God, unwilling to come under His wings?

translationNotes.note: A footnote records that several manuscripts read simply 'Cut it down' without the following clause; the sense is unchanged, the owner's patience has run out and judgment is due unless fruit appears.

The phrase rendered 'I will reach My goal' translates a Greek verb meaning to be completed or perfected. Luke uses it for the finishing of Jesus' God-appointed mission in His death and resurrection at Jerusalem, which no threat of Herod can hurry or prevent.
'Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord' quotes Psalm 118:26. It will be sung at the Triumphal Entry and points beyond it to the final recognition of Christ when He comes again.
